Hokay. So. Here's a special ed unmarried female teacher's perspective. Helping the needy isn't terrible. My kids are awesome. My hypothesis is that the burnout rate is high because of the actual system and legal threat in the special ed environment, not the kids. I can't tell you what it feels like to be that close to professional disaster all the time--it's a constant threat, constantly held over your head. Any slip, any moment of disorganization, any parent who has a hair trigger, and your professional life is over. That is not an exaggeration. If you flub an iep, if you flub monitoring a student's progress, if you miss a deadline, the families have lawyers stacked like planes on a runway to ruin you professionally. Your school will not support you. Your union will not support you. You only get support if you can prove that you didn't actually make a mistake or that the mistake was someone else's fault. There is literally one bad day's momentary lapse standing between you and never being able to teach again, and I'm not talking about sex offense or slapping a kid or gross physical neglect. I'm literally taking about paperwork. It's a fraught, over-legalized, fearful life to be a special ed teacher. I think people go into it, personally, because it fills a need. People have a need to feel like they're making a difference, people have a need to express themselves in a parental way, etc. But if you take a step back, ie maternity leave or a stint elsewhere, you realize just how close to the brink of disaster you felt professionally all the time. You don't go back.
